paper_metadata.title: Classical and quantum computing methods for estimating loan-level risk distributions

summary: The paper builds a classical Monte Carlo framework for loan-level lifetime default risk using Freddie Mac mortgage data (> $2T portfolio) and shows that the resulting lifetime PD distributions are well approximated by lognormal distributions, allowing estimation with ~50 simulations (~1.9 s per account) instead of 10,000. It then proposes a theoretical quantum Monte Carlo approach using quantum amplitude estimation with quadratic O(√M) sampling advantage, but no quantum experiment is executed and the full competing‑risks formulation would require about 4Nm qubits, exceeding near-term hardware.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo / quantum amplitude estimation for estimating lifetime probability of default under a simplified unconditional default-probability model for loan risk distributions.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo simulation with Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) following Egger et al./Woerner & Egger; bisection search for a target percentile

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each horizon t has an m-qubit register encoding the unconditional PD(t) distribution; registers are summed to form lifetime PD, and an indicator qubit marks whether the sum exceeds a threshold x for QAE.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the lifetime probability distribution / percentile (e.g., 95th percentile) of default probability from a sum of unconditional PD(t) distributions.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Threshold qubit C used to mark whether the summed value exceeds x; bisection search over x to find the desired percentile.

problem_instance.description: Loan-level risk distribution estimation for Freddie Mac mortgage accounts using a simplified unconditional default-probability model (not the full competing-risks model).

dataset_specification.description: 30-year fixed-rate conforming mortgages; account-level data including balance, delinquency, payments, payoff, origination date, origination score, postal code, LTV, DTI, number of borrowers, property type, and loan purpose

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Unconditional PD(t) modeled directly as booked-account default fraction; logit-normal distributions approximated by lognormal distributions for quantum loading; forecast horizon 36 months in the classical study, but the quantum section is described generically for N steps
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: The paper is conceptual/proof-of-principle for quantum feasibility; no hardware experiment or benchmark run is reported for the quantum algorithm

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo simulation used to estimate lifetime PD distributions; 10,000 simulations used for figures, and approximately 50 simulations are sufficient when fitting a lognormal distribution, giving runtime ≈1.9 seconds per account.
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Fit multihorizon survival/APC models; estimate unconditional PD(t) distributions; approximate logit-normal with lognormal for easier loading
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Bisection search over threshold x to recover percentile; QAE would estimate amplitude a corresponding to the target percentile

results.unit: classical error O(1/sqrt(M)); QAE error O(1/M)

speedup_claims.conditions: for quantum amplitude estimation applied to the simplified unconditional default-probability model; assuming the distribution can be loaded efficiently
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not execute a quantum circuit; it only argues that QAE can achieve O(1/M) error versus classical O(1/sqrt(M)) error, implying a square-root sample reduction.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(sqrt(M)) samples for amplitude estimation versus classical Monte Carlo
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(M) samples for Monte Carlo estimation of a target percentile; classical convergence rate described as O(1/sqrt(M)) error

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not specified; depends on number of Monte Carlo samples M and forecast horizon N
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires N registers of m qubits each plus support qubits for QAE; efficient distribution loading and sufficiently large M where quantum O(1/M) amplitude estimation scaling beats classical O(1/sqrt(M)).
limiting_factors: Quantum algorithm not executed on hardware
Efficient loading of probability distributions into amplitude registers is non‑trivial
Large qubit counts required for multiple forecast horizons
Error correction and coherence requirements not addressed

notes: The paper does not report an executed gate-based quantum hardware experiment; it only sketches a future quantum Monte Carlo/QAE implementation.
num_qubits is taken from the text stating N separate m-qubit registers are needed for the unconditional-distribution version.
No specific device, framework, shot count, or transpiled circuit metrics are reported.
The paper proposes a QAE-based Monte Carlo method but does not run it on a simulator or QPU.
Speedup discussed theoretically as quadratic relative to classical Monte Carlo.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo / amplitude estimation for the full competing-risks loan default model with conditional default and prepayment probabilities.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo simulation with QAE for competing-risks cash-flow model; entangled-copy/in-place register-saving discussion

problem_formulation.encoding_details: At each time step, conditional PD(t) and PA(t) distributions are loaded into m-qubit registers; an entangled copy of CPD(t) and a survival register S(t) are reused across steps to compute UPD(t)=CPD(t)·S(t).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the lifetime default distribution under a competing-risks model with conditional default and prepayment probabilities.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Entanglement via controlled gates is required so that reused registers remain perfectly correlated across calculations; no penalty formulation is used.

problem_instance.description: Loan-level competing-risks model for mortgage default and prepayment uncertainty using Freddie Mac mortgage data.

dataset_specification.description: 30-year fixed-rate conforming mortgages; competing risks between default and pay-off; multihorizon survival/APC model with environmental extrapolation via second-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Conditional PD and PA distributions derived from multihorizon survival models; confidence intervals on coefficients and environment forecasts assumed normal in logit space; Monte Carlo samples drawn from these distributions
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: The paper argues the full competing-risks quantum version is not yet feasible on near-term hardware; no quantum run is reported

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo simulation of the competing‑risks model used as the practical implementation; quantum competing‑risks algorithm analyzed theoretically only.
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Estimate APC lifecycle, vintage, and environment functions; fit panel logistic regressions; extrapolate environment with second-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Bisection search over threshold x would be used in a QAE setting to recover the desired percentile; not executed in the paper

results.unit: classical error O(1/sqrt(M)); QAE error O(1/M)

speedup_claims.conditions: for the full competing-risks loan default/prepayment model using QAE, if the required registers can be loaded and entangled efficiently
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the full competing-risks approach is significantly more complex than prior quantum VaR work and is beyond near-term hardware; it estimates 4Nm qubits in the best case and notes the approach would require additional algorithm development.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(M) samples for classical Monte Carlo

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not given; authors state hardware requirements exceed near-term devices
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Best‑case qubit requirement 4Nm plus supporting qubits for entangled registers across N forecast steps.
limiting_factors: Very large qubit requirement scaling as 4Nm
Need for entangled register copies across time steps
Competing‑risks dependency structure increases circuit size
No implemented circuit or resource estimates beyond rough scaling

notes: The paper explicitly states the full competing-risks quantum approach would require about 4Nm qubits in the best case and is beyond near-term hardware.
No actual gate-based hardware, simulator, or circuit metrics are reported for this experiment; it is a feasibility analysis only.
Section 3.6 explicitly states the competing‑risks version 'far exceeds the number of qubits available for commercial applications over the next couple of years.'
No execution or benchmark results are provided.
